kurals.tamil:
நாடாது நட்டலிற் கேடில்லை நட்டபின்
வீடில்லை நட்பாள் பவர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Naadaadhu nattalir kedillai nattapin
veedillai natpaal bavarkku.
kurals.meaning: Nothing does more harm than making friends without first looking into a person, because for those who truly keep faith with friendship, once a friend is made there is no getting free of the bond.
kurals.elementary: Imagine tying your shoelace to a friend’s shoelace for a three-legged race. Once the knot is tight, you have to run together wherever the other person goes. So before you tie the knot, make sure your partner is someone who runs the right way.
kurals.university: The chapter opens on a paradox: the very loyalty that makes a person a good friend is what makes a careless friendship dangerous. Natpaalbavar (நட்பாள்பவர்) are ‘those who maintain friendship’, people for whom a friend once made cannot be dropped; veedu (வீடு) here means ‘release’ or ‘leaving off’, not ‘house’. Parimelazhagar draws the inference the couplet implies: since the good never abandon a friend, there is no evil equal to friendship formed without naadal (நாடல், inquiry), and so the examination must come before, not after. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it the same way, while Kalaignar paraphrases it as ‘a bad friendship taken up without inquiry brings harm one cannot escape’. The text is the same in ytamizh, thirukkural.net and the sandhi-joined edition at thirukkural-thamizh.org.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Do not put your trust in a bad companion nor even trust an ordinary friend, for if he should get angry with you, he may bring all your secrets to light.”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya warns that trust given too freely, even to an ordinary friend, can be turned against you once the relationship sours.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts counsel caution before intimacy, because a bond once given cannot simply be taken back.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 2.6 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the caution, but Chanakya speaks of guarding secrets, not of the irreversibility of friendship.

christianity.quote_or_event: “If thou wouldst get a friend, try him before thou takest him, and do not credit him easily. For there is a friend for his own occasion, and he will not abide in the day of thy trouble.”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira tells his student to test a would-be friend before accepting him, because some friends stay only while it suits them. Sirach is deuterocanonical: it is Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians but not part of the Protestant or Jewish canon.
christianity.tie_back: Ben Sira and Valluvar give the same order of operations: test first, then befriend.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; the canonical status of Sirach differs across Christian traditions.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not take as intimates those other than yourselves, for they will not spare you [any] ruin.”
islam.explanation: The verse warns believers against taking as close confidants people whose hostility has already shown itself.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats a badly chosen intimate as a source of ruin and urges discernment before closeness.
islam._accuracy_note: The verse has a specific communal and political setting; the Kural’s point is general and personal.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jonathan and David bind themselves in a covenant of friendship, and the bond outlives Jonathan: years later David, now king, seeks out Jonathan’s lame son Mephibosheth and keeps him at his table for Jonathan’s sake.
judaism.explanation: In 1 Samuel 18 and 20 the two men swear a lasting covenant, and in 2 Samuel 9 David honours it even after Jonathan’s death.
judaism.tie_back: The story shows Valluvar’s premise from the positive side: a true friendship, once formed, is never released, which is exactly why it must be formed with care.
judaism._accuracy_note: Illustrates the binding nature of friendship but says nothing about prior investigation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “these four as enemies the wise behold, avoid them from afar as paths of peril.”
buddhism.explanation: After listing four kinds of foes who look like friends, the Buddha tells Sigala to recognise them and keep them at a distance.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha, like Valluvar, puts the discernment before the relationship: spot the false friend and avoid him from afar.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on avoiding bad friends early; it does not state that a friendship once made is irrevocable.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Let the wage promised to a friend be fixed; even with your brother smile—and get a witness; for trust and mistrust, alike ruin men.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod advises his brother Perses to keep clear terms even with friends and kin, because misplaced trust can ruin a man as surely as suspicion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod shares the Kural’s practical caution about giving trust before it has been earned.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 370-372 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Partial match: Hesiod is about prudence in dealings, not about choosing friends; also didactic poetry rather than myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, I must again and again repeat, you must satisfy your judgment before engaging your affections: not love first and judge afterwards.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius complains that people choose friends carelessly and then have to break off friendships later, when it is painful to do so.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero states Valluvar’s rule almost word for word: judge first, then love.
philosophy.source: Cicero, Laelius de Amicitia §22 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on the order of judging and loving.

kurals.tamil:
ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து கொள்ளாதான் கேண்மை கடைமுறை
தான்சாம் துயரம் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aaindhaaindhu kollaadhaan kenmai kadaimurai
thaansaam thuyaram tharum.
kurals.meaning: The friendship of someone who did not examine the other person again and again will in the end bring him grief bitter enough to kill him.
kurals.elementary: If you eat a mushroom from the woods without checking it, it might look fine today and make you very sick tomorrow. Friends are like that too. Look carefully, and then look again, before you let someone become your close friend.
kurals.university: The doubling aaindhu-aaindhu (ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து, ‘having examined and examined’) insists that a single check is not enough; Parimelazhagar understands it as examining a person by many means and on many occasions. Kenmai (கேண்மை) is intimate friendship, and kadaimurai (கடைமுறை) means ‘at the last’ or ‘in the final course’, so the harm is delayed, which is why it is so easily ignored. Thaan saam thuyaram (தான்சாம் துயரம்) is ‘a sorrow from which he himself dies’; most modern commentators, including Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar, take this as hyperbole for grief that can bring a person to death. The sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh.org reads தான்சாந் துயரந் தரும், a purely orthographic difference from the ytamizh and thirukkural.net texts.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Hitopadesha’s opening book, a deer befriends a smooth-talking jackal against the warning of his old friend the crow, who objects that one should not trust a newcomer whose nature is unknown; the jackal later lures the deer into a hunter’s snare hoping to feast on him, and only the crow’s cleverness saves the deer.
hinduism.explanation: The fable, part of the Mitralabha (‘Winning of Friends’), turns on a friendship accepted on a stranger’s pleasant words without any examination.
hinduism.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural’s warning that an unexamined friendship ends in mortal danger.
hinduism.source: Hitopadesha, Book I (Mitralabha), the deer, the crow and the jackal
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close narrative fit; summarised from memory of the tale rather than quoted, as no verified translation was checked.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go: Lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb warns against close friendship with a hot-tempered person because his ways become a trap for those who stay with him.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts see a poorly chosen friendship as a trap whose damage arrives later.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good thematic match; the proverb names one vice (anger) rather than calling for repeated examination.

islam.quote_or_event: “Oh, woe to me! I wish I had not taken that one as a friend. He led me away from the remembrance after it had come to me. And ever is Satan, to man, a deserter.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgment, the wrongdoer bites his hands and laments the friend who led him astray.
islam.tie_back: The verse paints exactly the Kural’s ‘grief at the last’: bitter regret over a friendship that should never have been formed.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close in the regret over a ruinous friendship; the Qur’an places the reckoning in the hereafter.

judaism.quote_or_event: Amnon, son of King David, has a friend named Jonadab, described as a very shrewd man, who devises the scheme by which Amnon wrongs his half-sister Tamar; two years later Absalom has Amnon killed in revenge.
judaism.explanation: The narrative in 2 Samuel 13 traces Amnon’s ruin back to the counsel of a clever but unscrupulous friend.
judaism.tie_back: It is a biblical case of the Kural’s point: a friend not judged by character leads at last to death.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel; the text does not itself moralise about choosing friends.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The man who has evil comrades and friends is given to evil ways, to ruin does he fall in both worlds — here and the next.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the young householder Sigala that bad companions drag a person into ruin in this life and the next.
buddhism.tie_back: The verse matches the Kural’s picture of a bad friendship ending in destruction.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on outcome; the sutta does not stress repeated testing.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pirithous, king of the Lapiths, meets Theseus and the two swear friendship on the spot. Bound by that oath, Theseus joins Pirithous’ reckless plan to carry off Persephone from the underworld; both are trapped in Hades, and while Heracles later frees Theseus, Pirithous is left there for ever.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth, told by Apollodorus and others, is the classic Greek case of a friendship sworn at first meeting and kept at ruinous cost.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shows how a friendship formed without scrutiny ends in deadly sorrow.
greek_mythology.source: Apollodorus, Library, Epitome 1.23-24; Plutarch, Life of Theseus 30-35
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong narrative fit; versions differ on whether Theseus is freed.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Further, such friendship requires time and familiarity; as the proverb says, men cannot know each other till they have ‘eaten salt together’ … for a wish for friendship may arise quickly, but friendship does not.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the best kind of friendship takes long acquaintance, because only time shows whether each person really deserves the other’s trust.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s ‘eating salt together’ is the long, repeated testing that the Kural’s aaindhu-aaindhu demands.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on the need for long testing; Aristotle does not dwell on the deadly outcome.

kurals.tamil:
குணமும் குடிமையும் குற்றமும் குன்றா
இனனும் அறிந்தியாக்க நட்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Gunamum kudimaiyum kutramum kundraa
inanum arindhiyaakka natpu.
kurals.meaning: Make friends with someone only after you know his character, his family background, his faults, and the circle of people he keeps close.
kurals.elementary: Before you join a new team, you watch how the players behave, who their coach is, what mistakes they make, and who they hang out with. Valluvar says to do the same four checks before you choose a close friend.
kurals.university: This couplet supplies the checklist for the chapter’s ‘investigation’: gunam (குணம், disposition or character), kudimai (குடிமை, lineage, the family in which one is raised), kutram (குற்றம், faults), and kundraa inam (குன்றா இனம், one’s abiding associates or kin). Parimelazhagar takes inam as the circle of relatives and companions who stand by a person, on the principle, developed in chapter 46 (Sitrinam Seraamai), that a person takes on the quality of the company he keeps; Puliyur Kesigan accordingly glosses it as ‘the companions who stay with him’. Arindhu yaakka (அறிந்து யாக்க) means ‘form it having known’. The ytamizh and thirukkural.net texts read குணமும், while the sandhi-joined edition reads குணனுங் குடிமையுங், an older spelling with the same meaning.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Ravana’s brother Vibhishana comes to Rama asking for refuge and friendship, Rama asks his counsellors for their views; Sugriva and others suspect a spy because of his lineage, while Hanuman argues from Vibhishana’s conduct and speech that he is sincere, and only after weighing these views does Rama accept him.
hinduism.explanation: The episode in the Yuddha Kanda is a formal inquiry into a would-be ally’s family, character and motives before a bond is formed.
hinduism.tie_back: Rama’s council examines exactly what the Kural lists: nature, lineage, possible faults and associations.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel; summarised rather than quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that a person’s true nature shows in what he produces, as a tree is known by its fruit.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say a person’s character must be read from evidence before you trust him.
christianity._accuracy_note: The context is false prophets, not friendship; the parallel is in method of judging.

islam.quote_or_event: “A man follows the religion of his friend; so each one should consider whom he makes his friend.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that a person takes on the ways of his close friend, so the choice of friend must be weighed carefully.
islam.tie_back: This hadith gives the reason for Valluvar’s checklist: you become like the people you befriend.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 4833 (graded hasan by al-Albani)
islam._accuracy_note: Very close match on examining a friend before choosing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Joshua said, a good companion; Rabbi Yose said, a good neighbor … Rabbi Joshua said, an evil companion; Rabbi Yose said, an evil neighbor”
judaism.explanation: Asked which path a person should cleave to and which he should shun, Rabban Yohanan’s disciples name the good or evil companion and neighbour among the deciding factors.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Mishnah treats the people around a person as something to examine and choose with care.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good thematic fit; the Mishnah lists qualities to cultivate rather than a checklist for vetting friends.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “These four, young householder, should be understood as foes in the guise of friends: (1) he who appropriates a friend’s possessions, (2) he who renders lip-service, (3) he who flatters, (4) he who brings ruin.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha gives Sigala a list of signs that reveal a false friend, each broken down into four observable behaviours.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the sutta turns friendship into something to be checked against specific marks of character.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close in method; the Buddha’s list concerns conduct, not family background.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On the battlefield before Troy, Diomedes asks the Lycian Glaucus who he is; Glaucus recites his lineage back to Bellerophon, and Diomedes realises their grandfathers were guest-friends, so instead of fighting they clasp hands, renew the friendship and exchange armour.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Iliad 6 an enemy becomes a friend only after his family and ancestral ties are laid out.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The episode shows the Kural’s concern with kudimai and inam: lineage and associations are checked before friendship is sealed.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on lineage; the episode is about inherited guest-friendship rather than testing character.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Now the qualities we ought to look out for in making our selection are firmness, stability, constancy. There is a plentiful lack of men so endowed, and it is difficult to form a judgment without testing.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero’s Laelius complains that people count their sheep carefully but choose friends with no criteria, and he names the qualities to look for.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero, like Valluvar, gives a checklist of character traits to verify before friendship.
philosophy.source: Cicero, Laelius de Amicitia §17 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on vetting character; Cicero does not list family or associates.

kurals.tamil:
குடிப்பிறந்து தன்கண் பழிநாணு வானைக்
கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் நட்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kudippirandhu thankan pazhinaanu vaanaik
koduththum kolalvendum natpu.
kurals.meaning: Win the friendship of a person raised in a good family who is ashamed at any hint of blame, even if it costs you something to do so.
kurals.elementary: Some friends are like a good umbrella: worth saving your pocket money for. A friend who comes from a caring home and feels bad if he does something wrong is that kind of friend, so it is worth giving up something to have him.
kurals.university: Kudippirandhu (குடிப்பிறந்து) means ‘born into a good family’, the kudi of chapter 96 (Kudimai), and pazhi naanuvaan (பழிநாணுவான்) is ‘one who feels shame at blame’, that is, someone whose sense of honour keeps him from disgraceful acts. Koduththum (கொடுத்தும், ‘even by giving’) carries the force of ‘even at a price’. Parimelazhagar takes it literally as giving wealth to secure such a friend, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah likewise say ‘even by paying a price’, while Kalaignar softens it to ‘by any means’. After three couplets of warning, the chapter turns here to the positive: some friendships are worth paying for. The ytamizh and thirukkural.net texts agree; the sandhi-joined edition reads தன்கட் and கொடுத்துங் … வேண்டு, orthographic variants only.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A man’s descent may be discerned by his conduct, his country by his pronunciation of language, his friendship by his warmth and glow”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya says that good birth shows itself in conduct, and true friendship in warmth.
hinduism.tie_back: Both link good family to visible good conduct; the Kural adds that such a person is worth acquiring as a friend.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 3.2 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the idea that lineage shows in conduct; does not urge paying to win such a friend.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A faithful friend is a strong defence: and he that hath found him, hath found a treasure. Nothing can be compared to a faithful friend, and no weight of gold and silver is able to countervail the goodness of his fidelity.”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira says a loyal friend is worth more than any amount of gold or silver. (Sirach is deuterocanonical, accepted by Catholic and Orthodox but not Protestant Christians.)
christianity.tie_back: Ben Sira and Valluvar both say a good friend is worth any price.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on the friend’s worth; Ben Sira stresses fidelity rather than family or sense of shame.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with those who are true.”
islam.explanation: The verse tells believers to keep company with the truthful.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural’s instruction to actively seek out people of integrity as companions.
islam._accuracy_note: General instruction on good company; no mention of family or of paying a price.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Joshua ben Perahiah used to say: appoint for thyself a teacher, and acquire for thyself a companion and judge all men with the scale weighted in his favor.”
judaism.explanation: The Hebrew verb here, k’neh, means ‘acquire’ or ‘buy’, and the rabbinic tradition (for example Avot de-Rabbi Natan) reads it as telling a person to obtain a good companion even at personal cost.
judaism.tie_back: This is the closest Jewish parallel to koduththum: a true companion is worth buying.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong verbal and conceptual match on ‘acquiring’ a friend; the Mishnah does not mention lineage.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, a friend endowed with seven qualities is worth associating with. Which seven? He gives what is hard to give. He does what is hard to do. He endures what is hard to endure. He reveals his secrets to you. He keeps your secrets. When misfortunes strike, he doesn’t abandon you. When you’re down & out, he doesn’t look down on you.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists seven qualities that make a person worth cultivating as a friend.
buddhism.tie_back: The sutta and the Kural agree that a friend of proven character is worth going out of your way to keep.
buddhism.source: Mitta Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya 7.35 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches the ‘worth having’ idea; the qualities differ from family and sense of shame.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pylades, a prince of Phocis raised alongside Orestes, stays with him through exile, madness and danger; in Euripides’ Iphigenia among the Taurians each insists on dying so that the other may live.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pylades was the Greek byword for the high-born, honourable friend who would pay any price for his companion.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is the kind of well-born, honour-bound friend the Kural says is worth securing at any cost.
greek_mythology.source: Euripides, Iphigenia among the Taurians; Aeschylus, Libation Bearers
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates the value of such a friend rather than the act of acquiring him.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But it is natural that such friendships should be infrequent; for such men are rare.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says friendship between good people is the best kind but is scarce, because good people themselves are scarce.
philosophy.tie_back: If such friends are rare, it follows, as the Kural says, that they are worth a high price.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Supports the rarity and value; Aristotle does not advise paying to obtain such friends.

kurals.tamil:
அழச்சொல்லி அல்லது இடித்து வழக்கறிய
வல்லார்நட்பு ஆய்ந்து கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Azhachcholli alladhu idiththu vazhakkariya
vallaarnatpu aaindhu kolal.
kurals.meaning: Look for and keep the friendship of people who can speak hard words that make you weep, or rebuke you sharply, and who understand how the world works.
kurals.elementary: A good coach sometimes tells you, ‘That was wrong, do it again,’ and it can make you want to cry. But that coach makes you better. Valluvar says to choose friends like that coach, not friends who only say nice things.
kurals.university: Azhach cholli (அழச்சொல்லி) is ‘speaking so as to make one weep’ and idiththu (இடித்து) is ‘striking’, that is, rebuking hard; the same verb appears in kural 448 of the idikkum thunai, the counsellor who rebukes a king. Parimelazhagar distinguishes the two: the friend makes you weep with counsel before a wrong is done, and rebukes you sharply after it is done; Solomon Pappaiah follows this two-step reading. Vazhakku ariya valla (வழக்கறிய வல்ல) means ‘able to make one know the ways of the world’, adding practical wisdom to frankness. Both ytamizh and thirukkural.net print வல்லார்நடபு, which is missing its pulli; the sandhi-joined edition’s வல்லார்நட் பாய்ந்து confirms the reading வல்லார்நட்பு used here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “They are abundant, O king, that can always speak agreeable words. The speaker, however, is rare, as also the hearer, of words that are disagreeable but medicinal.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura tells the blind king Dhritarashtra that flatterers are everywhere, but people who speak painful, healing truth are rare, and so are those willing to hear it.
hinduism.tie_back: Vidura’s ‘disagreeable but medicinal’ words are the hard words of the friend the Kural tells you to keep.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section XXXVII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close on the value of painful candour; framed as a counsellor to a king rather than a friend.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says a friend’s painful honesty can be trusted, while an enemy’s affection is a trick.
christianity.tie_back: The ‘wounds of a friend’ are the Kural’s words that make you weep.

islam.quote_or_event: “The believer is the believer’s mirror, and the believer is the believer’s brother who guards him against loss and protects him when he is absent.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet says a fellow believer should show you your faults as a mirror does, while also protecting you.
islam.tie_back: The ‘mirror’ friend who shows your faults is the Kural’s friend who rebukes.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 4918 (graded hasan by al-Albani)
islam._accuracy_note: Close on honest correction; the hadith is gentler and does not mention tears.

judaism.quote_or_event: “You shall not hate your kinsfolk in your heart. Reprove your kindred but incur no guilt on their account.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah makes rebuke a duty: instead of hating someone silently, you must tell him plainly where he is wrong.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts treat honest reproof as a mark of real love rather than a breach of it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on the duty of rebuke; the verse addresses kin and neighbours rather than chosen friends.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure. It is always better, and never worse, to cultivate such an association.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells his hearers to treat someone who points out their faults like a guide to buried treasure.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s own advice: seek out and keep the friend who rebukes.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: As the Greeks are being driven back to their ships, Patroclus comes to Achilles in tears and rebukes him as pitiless for sitting out the battle in anger while his comrades die, then begs to lead the Myrmidons himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: At the opening of Iliad 16, Achilles’ dearest friend is the one person who confronts him to his face over his wrath.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Patroclus is the friend who speaks hard words to stop a wrong, as the Kural describes.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good fit; here the friend weeps rather than making Achilles weep.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Plain speaking is a cause of trouble, if the result of it is resentment, which is poison of friendship; but compliance is really the cause of much more trouble, because by indulging his faults it lets a friend plunge into headlong ruin.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius argues that a friend who only goes along with you does more harm than one whose frankness stings.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero and Valluvar agree that the stinging, frank friend is the one worth keeping.
philosophy.source: Cicero, Laelius de Amicitia §24 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close match on frank reproof versus flattery.

kurals.tamil:
கேட்டினும் உண்டோர் உறுதி கிளைஞரை
நீட்டி அளப்பதோர் கோல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kettinum undor urudhi kilaignarai
neetti alappadhor kol.
kurals.meaning: Even misfortune has one benefit: it is a measuring rod that shows you, in full, how far your friends and kin really go for you.
kurals.elementary: When it rains, you find out which umbrellas have holes. When something bad happens to you, you find out which friends stay. That is the one good thing about a bad day: it shows you who your real friends are.
kurals.university: Kedu (கேடு) is ruin or misfortune and urudhi (உறுதி) is ‘benefit’ or ‘firm good’; the -um in kettinum gives ‘even in ruin’. Kilaignar (கிளைஞர்) literally means kin, ‘those of the same branch’, but Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators extend it to friends, since the chapter is about friendship. The image of neetti alappadhu oor kol (நீட்டி அளப்பதோர் கோல், ‘a rod that measures by stretching out’) is a surveyor’s measuring rod laid end to end, which measures exactly how far each person’s affection reaches. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both stress the paradox that harm itself becomes the instrument of knowledge. The sandhi-joined text reads கேட்டினு முண்டோ ருறுதி, the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Test a servant while in the discharge of his duty, a relative in difficulty, a friend in adversity, and a wife in misfortune.”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya says each kind of relationship has its own testing ground, and for a friend that test is adversity.
hinduism.tie_back: Chanakya makes the same claim as the Kural: hardship is the test that measures a friend.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 1.11 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)

christianity.quote_or_event: “A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says real friendship is constant and that hard times are what a brother is for.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say adversity is what reveals and proves a true friend or kinsman.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close; the proverb praises loyalty in adversity rather than calling adversity a measuring tool.

islam.quote_or_event: When the Prophet left Mecca under threat of death, Abu Bakr alone went with him and hid with him in the cave of Thawr while their pursuers searched nearby; the Qur’an remembers him as ‘the second of two’ to whom the Prophet said, ‘Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us.’
islam.explanation: Qur’an 9:40 recalls the Hijra, the moment of greatest danger, when Abu Bakr’s loyalty was proven.
islam.tie_back: The hour of danger showed who the true companion was, just as the Kural says misfortune measures friends.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong narrative illustration; paraphrased, not quoted verbatim.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But Ruth replied, ‘Do not urge me to leave you, to turn back and not follow you. For wherever you go, I will go; wherever you lodge, I will lodge; your people shall be my people, and your God my God.’”
judaism.explanation: Widowed and destitute, Naomi urges her daughters-in-law to go home; Orpah leaves, but Ruth refuses to abandon her.
judaism.tie_back: Naomi’s ruin works as the Kural’s measuring rod: it shows who stays and who goes.
judaism._accuracy_note: Excellent narrative fit; it concerns kin by marriage rather than chosen friends, which suits kilaignar.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who is the same in happiness and sorrow be understood as a warm-hearted friend: (i) he reveals his secrets, (ii) he conceals one’s own secrets, (iii) in misfortune he does not forsake one, (iv) his life even he sacrifices for one’s sake.”
buddhism.explanation: Among the marks of a true friend, the Buddha lists that he does not leave you when misfortune comes.
buddhism.tie_back: The Buddha and Valluvar both name misfortune as the moment a true friend is recognised.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close; the sutta lists the trait rather than calling misfortune a test.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus comes home to Ithaca disguised as a ragged beggar and uses his apparent ruin to test his household: the swineherd Eumaeus shares his meagre food with him, while the goatherd Melanthius kicks and insults him, and the loyalty of each is revealed.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the second half of the Odyssey, Odysseus deliberately takes on the look of misfortune in order to measure who is faithful.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His disguise turns misfortune into exactly the Kural’s measuring rod for friends and dependants.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very apt narrative; the misfortune is staged rather than real.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And though what Ennius says is quite true,—‘the hour of need shews the friend indeed,’—yet it is in these two ways that most people betray their untrustworthiness and inconstancy”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius quotes the poet Ennius’ line, the source of the English proverb ‘a friend in need is a friend indeed’, and adds that prosperity and adversity both expose false friends.
philosophy.tie_back: Ennius’ ‘hour of need’ is the Kural’s measuring rod of misfortune.
philosophy.source: Cicero, Laelius de Amicitia §17, quoting Ennius (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on adversity revealing friends.

kurals.tamil:
ஊதியம் என்பது ஒருவற்குப் பேதையார்
கேண்மை ஒரீஇ விடல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Oodhiyam enbadhu oruvarkup pedhaiyaar
kenmai oreei vidal.
kurals.meaning: The real gain for a person is to give up, completely, his friendship with fools.
kurals.elementary: If your kite is tied to a heavy rock, it can never fly. Cutting the string to the rock is not a loss; it is how the kite goes up. Letting go of a friend who keeps pulling you into silly trouble is the same kind of win.
kurals.university: Oodhiyam (ஊதியம்) is ‘profit’ or ‘gain’, a deliberately commercial word in a chapter of the Porutpal. Pedhaiyaar (பேதையார்) are fools in the specific Kural sense defined in chapter 84 (Pedhaimai): people who take up what harms them and drop what helps them. Oreei (ஒரீஇ) is an alapedai (sound-lengthened) form of oruvi, ‘having abandoned’, and with vidal (விடல், ‘letting go’) it makes ‘to abandon and let go entirely’. Parimelazhagar and Puliyur Kesigan read the couplet as applying to a friendship already formed with a fool unknowingly: leaving it as soon as the folly is recognised is itself a gain. The sandhi-joined text reads ஊதிய மென்ப தொருவற்குப் … யொரீஇ, the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Do not keep company with a fool for as we can see he is a two-legged beast. Like an unseen thorn he pierces the heart with his sharp words.”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya warns that a fool’s company wounds you in ways you do not see coming.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say that staying away from fools is to your benefit.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 3.7 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close in counsel; harsher in tone and silent on the idea of ‘gain’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb contrasts the gain of walking with the wise with the loss suffered by the friend of fools.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts frame leaving fools’ company as profit and keeping it as loss.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of a good companion (who sits with you) in comparison with a bad one, is like that of the musk seller and the blacksmith’s bellows (or furnace); from the first you would either buy musk or enjoy its good smell while the bellows would either burn your clothes or your house, or you get a bad nasty smell thereof.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares a good companion to a perfume seller whose fragrance you share, and a bad one to a blacksmith whose sparks burn you.
islam.tie_back: Both texts weigh companions in terms of gain and loss.
islam._accuracy_note: Same gain-and-loss logic; the hadith speaks of bad rather than specifically foolish companions.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Keep your distance from a dull man, For you will not learn wise speech.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb advises walking away from a fool, since nothing wise can be gained from him.
judaism.tie_back: Both say that leaving the fool is the sensible, profitable choice.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match; the translator notes an alternative rendering of the first line.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should a seeker not find a companion who is better or equal, let him resolutely pursue a solitary course; there is no fellowship with the fool.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says it is better to walk alone than to keep company with a fool.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the verse treats leaving the fool, even for solitude, as the better bargain.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The Farmer laughed aloud and said, ‘It may be all as you say, I only know this: I have taken you with these robbers, the Cranes, and you must die in their company.’”
greek_mythology.explanation: A stork caught in a net with crop-stealing cranes pleads its good character, but the farmer judges it by the company it was keeping.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The fable shows the cost of not leaving bad company in time, the loss the Kural tells us to avoid.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, The Farmer and the Stork (trans. G. F. Townsend)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A fable rather than myth; the cranes are thieves rather than fools.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But wicked men have no steadfastness (for they do not remain even like to themselves), but become friends for a short time because they delight in each other’s wickedness.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says friendships among bad people are short and unstable because they rest on shared vice.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle explains why such a friendship is worth nothing and losing it is no loss.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.8 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Concerns the wicked rather than fools, and does not counsel leaving them.

kurals.tamil:
உள்ளற்க உள்ளம் சிறுகுவ கொள்ளற்க
அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார் நட்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ullarka ullam sirukuva kollarka
allarkan aatraruppaar natpu.
kurals.meaning: Do not dwell on things that shrink your spirit, and do not take up the friendship of people who will abandon you when trouble comes.
kurals.elementary: Some friends are like a bicycle that only works on sunny days: the moment it rains, the chain falls off. Do not count on a friend like that. Pick friends who will still be pedalling with you when the road gets muddy.
kurals.university: The couplet sets two prohibitions side by side. Ullarka ullam siruguva (உள்ளற்க உள்ளம் சிறுகுவ) is ‘do not think the things that make the mind small’; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take this as avoiding whatever saps one’s energy and resolve (ookkam), and Parimelazhagar treats the first line as an analogy for the second: just as one should not entertain spirit-shrinking thoughts, one should not take up such friends. Allarkan aatraruppaar (அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார்) are ‘those who cut off the way in time of distress’, people who withdraw their support exactly when it is needed. Puliyur Kesigan reads the first line differently, as a warning not to think meanly of a friend, which shows the line is open to more than one interpretation. The sandhi-joined text reads உள்ளற்க வுள்ளஞ் … வல்லற்க ணாற்றறுப்பார், the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He is a true friend who does not forsake us in time of need, misfortune, famine, or war, in a king’s court, or at the crematorium (smasana).”
hinduism.explanation: Chanakya lists the hard places where a true friend still stands beside you.
hinduism.tie_back: Chanakya defines the true friend by the same test the Kural uses: he does not leave in times of trouble.
hinduism.source: Chanakya Niti 1.12 (Sri Chanakya Niti-sastra, English translation)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close match; it states the positive form of the Kural’s prohibition.

christianity.quote_or_event: “At my first answer no man stood with me, but all men forsook me: I pray God that it may not be laid to their charge.”
christianity.explanation: Writing from prison, Paul recalls that at his first hearing his supporters deserted him.
christianity.tie_back: Paul describes the very friends the Kural warns against: those who vanish in the hour of distress.
christianity._accuracy_note: Vivid illustration; Paul responds with forgiveness rather than advice to avoid such friends.

islam.quote_or_event: “[The hypocrites are] like the example of Satan when he says to man, ‘Disbelieve.’ But when he disbelieves, he says, ‘Indeed, I am disassociated from you. Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds.’”
islam.explanation: The verse compares false allies to Satan, who urges a person into wrongdoing and then disowns him when the consequences arrive.
islam.tie_back: It describes the companion who abandons you at the moment of trouble.
islam._accuracy_note: Theological setting; the parallel lies in the desertion, not in friendship advice.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Be careful [in your dealings] with the ruling authorities for they do not befriend a person except for their own needs; they seem like friends when it is to their own interest, but they do not stand by a man in the hour of his distress.”
judaism.explanation: Rabban Gamaliel warns that powerful patrons seem friendly while it serves them but are gone when trouble comes.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s deserting friend, described almost in its own words.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close on desertion in distress; aimed specifically at the ruling powers.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who renders lip-service be understood as a foe in the guise of a friend: (i) he makes friendly profession as regards the past, (ii) he makes friendly profession as regards the future, (iii) he tries to gain one’s favor by empty words, (iv) when opportunity for service has arisen, he expresses his inability.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the false friend who talks warmly but is never available when help is actually needed.
buddhism.tie_back: The lip-service friend is the one who, in the Kural’s words, cuts off the way in time of trouble.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close; the sutta adds the empty-words element.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He gave me this advice,” his companion replied. “Never travel with a friend who deserts you at the approach of danger.”
greek_mythology.explanation: When a bear appears, one traveller scrambles up a tree and leaves his companion to save himself by playing dead.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The fable gives the Kural’s own advice: do not keep a friend who runs at the first sign of danger.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop, The Bear and the Two Travelers (trans. G. F. Townsend)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; a fable rather than myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Those who are friends for the sake of utility part when the advantage is at an end; for they were lovers not of each other but of profit.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle explains that friendships based on usefulness dissolve as soon as one party is no longer useful.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle gives the reason fair-weather friends desert: they never loved the person, only the benefit.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.4 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in diagnosis; Aristotle analyses rather than forbids.

kurals.tamil:
கெடுங்காலைக் கைவிடுவார் கேண்மை அடுங்காலை
உள்ளினும் உள்ளஞ் சுடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kedungaalaik kaividuvaar kenmai adungaalai
ullinum ullanj chudum.
kurals.meaning: The memory of friends who abandoned you when you were falling will burn your heart, even if it comes back to you at the hour of death.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever been left alone by a friend when you really needed help? That hurt can stay with you for a very long time, even when you are grown up. Valluvar says this hurt is so strong it can burn even at the very end of life.
kurals.university: Kedungaalai (கெடுங்காலை) is ‘at the time when one is being ruined’, and adungaalai (அடுங்காலை) is ‘at the time when one is being slain’, the hour of death; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as the time when Yama comes to kill, and Kalaignar reads it as the moment one is being put to death. Ullinum (உள்ளினும், ‘even if one recalls’) and ullam sudum (உள்ளம் சுடும், ‘the heart burns’) make a play on ul- (‘think’) and ullam (‘mind’). The force of the couplet is psychological: the wound of desertion outlasts every other pain, so one should never form such a friendship in the first place, which ties it back to the chapter’s theme of investigation. The sandhi-joined text reads கேண்மை யடுங்காலை யுள்ளினு முள்ளஞ் சுடும், the same words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Drona and Drupada were boyhood friends, and Drupada promised to share his kingdom one day; when the impoverished Drona later came to him, King Drupada scorned him, saying friendship is impossible between a king and a poor man. The humiliation burned in Drona for years, until he had his pupils, the Kuru princes, capture Drupada and paid him back by taking half his kingdom.
hinduism.explanation: In the Adi Parva, a friend’s rejection in a time of need leaves a wound that shapes Drona’s whole life and feeds the feud behind the great war.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the Kural’s burning memory of a friend who abandoned you when you were down.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel; summarised from the epic, not quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “To him that is afflicted pity should be shewed from his friend; but he forsaketh the fear of the Almighty. My brethren have dealt deceitfully as a brook, and as the stream of brooks they pass away;”
christianity.explanation: In his suffering, Job complains that his friends have failed him like seasonal streams that dry up just when they are needed.
christianity.tie_back: Job voices the burning pain of friends who fail in the time of ruin.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close in feeling; Job’s friends stay present but fail in sympathy.

islam.quote_or_event: “Close friends, that Day, will be enemies to each other, except for the righteous”
islam.explanation: The verse says that on the Day of Judgment friendships not built on righteousness will turn into hostility.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it looks ahead to the final hour, when unworthy friendships are remembered with bitterness.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the ‘final hour’ frame; the Qur’an speaks of the hereafter rather than personal desertion.

judaism.quote_or_event: “All love that depends on a something, [when the] thing ceases, [the] love ceases; and [all love] that does not depend on anything, will never cease. What is an example of love that depended on a something? Such was the love of Amnon for Tamar. And what is an example of love that did not depend on anything? Such was the love of David and Jonathan.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah explains that love based on some benefit vanishes when the benefit does, while unconditional love lasts.
judaism.tie_back: It explains why the deserting friend left: his love depended on your good fortune, and when that ended, so did he.
judaism._accuracy_note: Explains conditional love well; does not speak of the pain of remembering it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is a bottle friend; one says, ‘friend, friend’ only to one’s face; one is a friend and an associate only when it is advantageous.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes friends who are present only for drinking, flattery or advantage.
buddhism.tie_back: These are the friends who leave when ruin comes, whom the Kural says will burn in memory.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Describes the type of friend but not the lasting pain of desertion.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On the way to Troy, the Greek leaders abandon the wounded archer Philoctetes alone on the island of Lemnos because his festering wound is unbearable to them; in Sophocles’ play, ten years later, his bitterness toward Odysseus and the sons of Atreus is still so fierce that he would rather die than help them.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sophocles’ Philoctetes is an extended study of the lasting resentment of a man deserted by his comrades in his worst hour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His undying anger is the Kural’s burning heart, kindled by friends who left him when he was falling.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel; summarised rather than quoted.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “it is in these two ways that most people betray their untrustworthiness and inconstancy, by looking down on friends when they are themselves prosperous, or deserting them in their distress.”
philosophy.explanation: Laelius names deserting a friend in distress as one of the two commonest betrayals of friendship.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero names the very betrayal whose memory, the Kural says, burns at the last.
philosophy.source: Cicero, Laelius de Amicitia §17 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the betrayal; does not describe the lasting pain.

kurals.tamil:
மருவுக மாசற்றார் கேண்மைஒன் றீத்தும்
ஒருவுக ஒப்பிலார் நட்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Maruvuka maasatraar kenmaion reeththum
oruvuka oppilaar natpu.
kurals.meaning: Hold close the friendship of the blameless, and get out of the friendship of the unsuitable, even if you have to give something up to do it.
kurals.elementary: Think of friends like food. Keep eating the fresh fruit. If something in your lunchbox has gone bad, throw it away, even if you paid for it. Keep good friends close, and let the bad ones go even if that costs you something.
kurals.university: The closing couplet balances two imperatives in parallel: maruvuka (மருவுக, ‘cling to, embrace’) and oruvuka (ஒருவுக, ‘leave, shun’). Maasatraar (மாசற்றார்) are ‘those without stain’, while oppilaar (ஒப்பிலார்) is ambiguous: Parimelazhagar takes it as those who do not accord with the world’s good ways, Solomon Pappaiah follows with ‘those who do not fit with the world’, and Mu. Varadarasanar reads ‘those who lack matching virtue’. Onru eeththum (ஒன்று ஈத்தும், ‘even by giving something’) mirrors koduththum in kural 794: just as a good friend is worth buying, a bad one is worth paying to be rid of. The ytamizh and thirukkural.net texts read ஈத்தும், while the sandhi-joined edition divides the line as கேண்மையொன் றீத்து மொருவுக, which reads the same once the sandhi is undone.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Old age killeth beauty; patience, hope; death, life; the practice of virtue, worldly enjoyments; lust, modesty; companionship with the wicked, good behaviour; anger, prosperity; and pride, everything.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura lists things that destroy other things, including bad company destroying good conduct.
hinduism.tie_back: It gives the reason the Kural says to leave unsuitable friends at any cost: bad company eats away at good conduct.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section XXXVII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Gives the reason for leaving bad company; it does not urge clinging to the blameless.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.”
christianity.explanation: Paul quotes a proverb, found earlier in the Greek poet Menander, warning that bad company corrupts good character.
christianity.tie_back: Paul and Valluvar both warn that the wrong friends corrupt, so they must be left behind.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on the danger; lacks the positive half about clinging to the pure.

islam.quote_or_event: “And keep yourself patient [by being] with those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, seeking His countenance … and do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance and who follows his desire and whose affair is ever [in] neglect.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet is told to stay with the sincere worshippers and not to follow the heedless.
islam.tie_back: The verse has the same two halves as the Kural: hold fast to the pure, turn from the unworthy.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the two-part structure; framed religiously and without the idea of paying a price.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Nittai the Arbelite used to say: keep a distance from an evil neighbor, do not become attached to the wicked, and do not abandon faith in [divine] retribution.”
judaism.explanation: Nittai of Arbel tells his students to keep away from bad neighbours and not to bind themselves to the wicked.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s second imperative, ‘shun the unsuitable’, in rabbinic form.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close on shunning; Avot 1:6 supplies the positive half of acquiring a good companion.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Do not associate with evil companions; do not seek the fellowship of the vile. Associate with the good friends; seek the fellowship of noble men.”
buddhism.explanation: The verse sets avoidance of evil companions directly beside the seeking of noble friends.
buddhism.tie_back: Its two halves mirror the Kural’s maruvuka and oruvuka almost exactly.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one structural match; lacks the ‘even at a price’.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “A bad neighbour is as great a plague as a good one is a great blessing; he who enjoys a good neighbour has a precious possession. Not even an ox would die but for a bad neighbour.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells Perses that the people living closest to you are either a blessing or a plague.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, Hesiod puts the good associate and the bad one side by side and counts the first as a treasure.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 346-348 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Neighbours rather than chosen friends; didactic poetry rather than myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Perfect friendship is the friendship of men who are good, and alike in virtue; for these wish well alike to each other qua good, and they are good themselves.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says the highest friendship exists only between good people who are alike in virtue.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s ‘alike in virtue’ is the opposite of the Kural’s oppilaar, the unlike or unfit whose friendship should be left.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on clinging to the virtuous; implicit rather than explicit on leaving the unfit.
